stem: An engineer is configuring a new Cilium cluster and wants to ensure that TCP workloads are optimized using BBR congestion control. According to the documentation, what is a prerequisite for enabling BBR congestion control for Pods?

options.text: Enabling the bandwidth manager
Installing the bandwidth CNI plugin
Configuring TBF (Token Bucket Filter) on the host
Disabling BPF Host Routing

explanation: The source explicitly states that "Cilium's bandwidth manager is also prerequisite for enabling BBR congestion control for Pods". It also notes that the bandwidth CNI plugin is not used and that TBF is not recommended.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states that the bandwidth manager "does not make use of the bandwidth CNI plugin" and that it is "not recommended to use the bandwidth CNI plugin".
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that the bandwidth CNI plugin is based on TBF and is not recommended, whereas the bandwidth manager uses EDT.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt strongly recommends using the Bandwidth Manager in combination with BPF Host Routing, not disabling it.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote: Cilium's bandwidth manager is also prerequisite for enabling BBR congestion control for Pods as outlined below.

stem: A cluster administrator is troubleshooting latency issues in a Cilium cluster where the bandwidth manager is enabled. They observe that traffic is being routed through the upper stack, resulting in undesired high latency. According to the documentation, what configuration is strongly recommended to avoid this issue?

options.text: Using the bandwidth CNI plugin
Using Bandwidth Manager in combination with BPF Host Routing
Disabling the bandwidth manager
Using TBF (Token Bucket Filter) for rate limiting

explanation: The excerpt states: "It is strongly recommended to use Bandwidth Manager in combination with BPF Host Routing as otherwise legacy routing through the upper stack could potentially result in undesired high latency".

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states that the bandwidth manager does not rely on CNI chaining and does not make use of the bandwidth CNI plugin.
optionRationale.c: Disabling the bandwidth manager would not address the routing issue described, which is related to the interaction between the bandwidth manager and routing modes.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states that TBF is not recommended due to scalability concerns, and the issue described is related to routing, not the specific rate-limiting algorithm.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote: It is strongly recommended to use Bandwidth Manager in combination with BPF Host Routing as otherwise legacy routing through the upper stack could potentially result in undesired high latency

stem: An engineer is configuring the bandwidth manager for a multi-node cluster. They need to manually specify the network devices on which egress bandwidth limitation is enforced because the auto-detection is not suitable for their setup. Which Helm option should they use to specify the device names?

options.text: The `devices` helm option
The `bandwidth` helm option
The `egress-bandwidth` annotation
The `ingress-bandwidth` annotation

explanation: The excerpt states: "To change and manually specify the devices, set their names in the `devices` helm option (e.g. `devices='eth0,eth1,eth2'`)".

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not mention a `bandwidth` helm option for specifying devices; it mentions the `devices` option.
optionRationale.c: The `egress-bandwidth` annotation is used to set the bandwidth limit for a Pod, not to specify the network devices for the bandwidth manager.
optionRationale.d: The `ingress-bandwidth` annotation is used to set the bandwidth limit for a Pod, not to specify the network devices for the bandwidth manager.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote: To change and manually specify the devices, set their names in the ``devices`` helm option (e.g. ``devices='eth0,eth1,eth2'``).

stem: An engineer wants to use a pool name other than `default` for the migration from cluster-pool to multi-pool IPAM. According to the provided procedure, how should this be configured?

options.text: By setting the `ipam.operator.autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools.<pool-name>` parameters in the Helm upgrade command.
By using the flag `--set-string extraConfig.ipam-default-ip-pool=<pool-name>` in the same Helm upgrade that restarts the operator.
By manually creating a `CiliumPodIPPool` resource with the desired name before running the Helm upgrade.
By modifying the `spec.ipam.podCIDRs` field in the `CiliumNode` resources to reference the new pool name.

explanation: The excerpt explicitly states: 'If you want to use a different default pool name for the migration, configure it globally in the same Helm upgrade that restarts the operator, with `--set-string extraConfig.ipam-default-ip-pool=<pool-name>`.'

optionRationale.a: The `ipam.operator.autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools` parameter is used to define the CIDR and mask size for the pool, but the specific flag for changing the *name* of the default pool is `extraConfig.ipam-default-ip-pool`.
optionRationale.c: The procedure relies on the operator to create the pool automatically (`autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools`), not on manual creation beforehand.
optionRationale.d: The `CiliumNode` resources are updated *after* the migration by the operator; they are not used to configure the migration target pool name.

citations.title: Practical Example
citations.quote: If you want to use a different default pool name for the migration, configure it globally in the same Helm upgrade that restarts the operator, with ``--set-string extraConfig.ipam-default-ip-pool=<pool-name>``.

The pods remain on Node Group 1 but are assigned new IP addresses from the 10.20.0.0/16 CIDR.
The pods are deleted and must be manually recreated to obtain IP addresses from the new pool.
The pods are rescheduled to Node Group 2 but retain their original IP addresses from the 10.10.0.0/16 CIDR.

explanation: The excerpt states that after draining Node Group 1, the nginx pod running on kind-worker (Node Group 1) is rescheduled on kind-control-plane (Node Group 2) with an IP address from the updated pool (10.20.11.182, which is within 10.20.0.0/16).

optionRationale.b: Incorrect because the nodes in Node Group 1 are cordoned and drained, so pods cannot remain on them.
optionRationale.c: Incorrect because the pods are rescheduled, not deleted and manually recreated.
optionRationale.d: Incorrect because the new pods receive IP addresses from the updated pool, not the old one.

stem: An engineer executes the command `kubectl exec "$FORTIO_POD" -c fortio -- /usr/bin/fortio load -c 2 -qps 0 -n 20 http://echo-service:8080`. Based on the provided output, what is the distribution of HTTP response codes received?

options.text: 19 requests returned code 200 and 1 request returned code 503.
20 requests returned code 200 and 0 requests returned code 503.
10 requests returned code 200 and 10 requests returned code 503.
18 requests returned code 200 and 2 requests returned code 503.

explanation: The output for the command with `-c 2` explicitly states `Code 200 : 19 (95.0 %)` and `Code 503 : 1 (5.0 %)`. This indicates that out of the 20 total calls, 19 were successful and 1 triggered the circuit breaker with a 503 error.

optionRationale.b: Incorrect. The output clearly shows one instance of `Code 503 : 1 (5.0 %)`, so not all requests were successful.
optionRationale.c: Incorrect. The output shows 19 successful requests, not 10. The 50% split is not supported by the data.
optionRationale.d: Incorrect. The output shows only one 503 error, not two. The count for code 200 is 19, not 18.

optionRationale.b: Incorrect. The logs specify `"code":"503"`, not 500.
optionRationale.c: Incorrect. The logs specify `"code":"503"`, not 429.
optionRationale.d: Incorrect. The logs specify `"code":"503"`, not 502.

stem: An engineer is testing the L7 circuit breaker and observes that with 2 concurrent connections, only 1 out of 20 requests fails with a 503 error. When the engineer increases the concurrency to 4 connections, the output shows multiple 503 errors. According to the excerpt, what does the presence of the 503 response code indicate?

options.text: It indicates that the circuit breaker has been triggered.
It indicates that the Fortio client has crashed.
It indicates that the echo-service is completely down.
It indicates that the Kubernetes pod is restarting.

explanation: The excerpt explicitly states: "From the above output, you can see that the response code of some requests is 503, which triggers a circuit breaker." Therefore, the 503 code is the indicator that the circuit breaker mechanism has activated.

optionRationale.b: Incorrect. The Fortio client continues to run and report statistics; it does not crash.
optionRationale.c: Incorrect. The service is not completely down, as some requests (or in the first test, most) still return 200, and the 503 is specifically linked to the circuit breaker, not total unavailability.
optionRationale.d: Incorrect. There is no mention of pod restarts in the output or explanation.

stem: An engineer applies a `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` to deny all traffic by default. When an external client sends a request to the `/details` endpoint, the response is a 403 Forbidden. According to the Hubble flow logs provided, what is the status of the HTTP request flow?

options.text: DROPPED
FORWARDED
ALLOWED
DENIED

explanation: The Hubble output explicitly shows the line `http-request DROPPED (HTTP/1.1 GET http://172.19.255.194/details/1)`. Although the client receives a 403 response, the flow status for the request itself is recorded as DROPPED.

optionRationale.b: FORWARDED is the status of the http-response, not the http-request.
optionRationale.c: ALLOWED is not the specific status shown in the log for the dropped request.
optionRationale.d: DENIED is a general concept but the specific log status is DROPPED.

stem: The documentation suggests a specific approach for allowing ingress traffic to the `/details` endpoint. Why is it considered more reliable to allow all traffic from the `reserved:ingress` identity to all `cluster` identities rather than allowing egress to specific identities?

options.text: Because Cilium Ingress is part of the networking infrastructure.
Because it reduces the number of policy rules required.
Because it prevents external traffic from reaching the cluster.
Because it ensures that all HTTP requests are encrypted.

explanation: The text states: "But in general, it's probably more reliable to allow all traffic from the `reserved:ingress` identity to all `cluster` identities, given that Cilium Ingress is part of the networking infrastructure."

optionRationale.b: The text does not mention rule count as the reason for reliability.
optionRationale.c: Allowing traffic from reserved:ingress to cluster does not prevent external traffic; it manages how the ingress gateway communicates with the cluster.
optionRationale.d: Encryption is not mentioned in the context of this policy decision.

stem: An engineer is deploying Cilium 1.16 in a development environment where a LoadBalancer Service is unavailable. They enable the Cilium Gateway API host network mode via Helm. What is the immediate effect on the LoadBalancer type Service mode?

options.text: The LoadBalancer type Service mode is automatically disabled because the two modes are mutually exclusive.
The LoadBalancer type Service mode remains active, allowing traffic to be routed through both the host network and the LoadBalancer simultaneously.
The LoadBalancer type Service mode is converted into a NodePort Service to maintain compatibility with the host network configuration.
The LoadBalancer type Service mode is paused until the host network mode is explicitly disabled by the administrator.

explanation: The source states that enabling the Cilium Gateway API host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer type Service mode, as they are mutually exclusive.

optionRationale.b: Incorrect because the modes are mutually exclusive; they cannot be active simultaneously.
optionRationale.c: Incorrect because the LoadBalancer mode is disabled, not converted. The conversion to NodePort applies to the Service generated for TCPRoute and UDPRoute, not the primary LoadBalancer mode.
optionRationale.d: Incorrect because the mode is disabled automatically, not paused.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: Enabling the Cilium Gateway API host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer type Service mode. They are mutually exclusive.

stem: A cluster administrator configures a Gateway with a TCPRoute in an environment where Cilium host network mode is enabled. How does the traffic for this TCPRoute behave compared to standard Gateway listener traffic?

options.text: The traffic bypasses Envoy and reaches the Gateway's generated Service directly, which is converted to a NodePort Service with a randomly assigned port.
The traffic is processed by Envoy and exposed on the host network using the port configured in the Gateway listener specification.
The traffic is blocked entirely because host network mode is incompatible with all route types, including TCPRoute.
The traffic bypasses Envoy but is exposed on the host network using the exact port configured on the Gateway listener.

explanation: The source explains that host network mode is not compatible with TCPRoute and UDPRoute. Their traffic bypasses Envoy and reaches the Gateway's generated Service directly. Enabling host network mode turns this Service into a NodePort Service, which gets a randomly assigned port from the node port range rather than the port configured on the Gateway listener.

optionRationale.b: Incorrect because TCPRoute traffic bypasses Envoy in this mode and does not use the configured listener port on the host network.
optionRationale.c: Incorrect because the traffic is not blocked; it is routed via a NodePort Service, albeit with a different port.
optionRationale.d: Incorrect because the port is randomly assigned from the node port range, not the configured listener port.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: Host network mode is not compatible with ``TCPRoute`` and ``UDPRoute``. Their traffic bypasses Envoy and reaches the Gateway's generated Service directly, which normally exposes the configured ``Gateway`` listener port as a ``LoadBalancer`` Service. Enabling host network mode turns this Service into a ``NodePort`` Service instead, which gets a randomly assigned port from the node port range rather than the port configured on the ``Gateway`` listener.

stem: When configuring a Gateway for Cilium host network mode, what constraint applies to the port specified in `spec.listeners.port`?

options.text: The port must be unique per Gateway resource and should be higher than 1023.
The port must be unique across all namespaces and must be lower than 1024 to ensure privileged access.
The port can be any value between 1 and 65535, provided it is not already used by a LoadBalancer Service.
The port must be identical to the port used by the associated NodePort Service for TCPRoute traffic.

explanation: The source states that the port must be unique per Gateway resource and that you should choose a port number higher than 1023.

optionRationale.b: Incorrect because the port should be higher than 1023, not lower, and uniqueness is per Gateway resource, not necessarily across all namespaces in the context of the specific constraint mentioned.
optionRationale.c: Incorrect because the source specifically advises choosing a port higher than 1023 to avoid privileged port issues.
optionRationale.d: Incorrect because the NodePort for TCPRoute is randomly assigned, so it will not match the configured listener port.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: The port must be unique per ``Gateway`` resource and you should choose a port number higher than ``1023`` (see `Bind to privileged port`_).

stem: In a Cilium cluster with host network mode enabled, how are the node addresses in the `GatewayStatusAddress` field handled to ensure consistency?

options.text: Cilium automatically sorts the node addresses to ensure that the same addresses are selected, within a maximum of 16 addresses.
The addresses are selected randomly from the available nodes to distribute load evenly across the cluster.
Only the address of the node where the Gateway resource is defined is included in the status field.
The addresses are sorted alphabetically by node name to allow for easy manual verification by administrators.

explanation: The source states that Cilium with host network mode enabled will automatically sort the node addresses to allow for consistency, ensuring that the same addresses are selected, and notes that the field has a maximum of 16 addresses.

optionRationale.b: Incorrect because the addresses are sorted for consistency, not selected randomly.
optionRationale.c: Incorrect because the status field contains node addresses (up to 16), not just the defining node.
optionRationale.d: Incorrect because the source specifies sorting for consistency of selection, not alphabetical sorting by name.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: The ``GatewayStatusAddress`` field for a gateway has a maximum of 16 addresses. Cilium with host network mode enabled will automatically sort the node addresses to allow for consistency, ensuring that the same addresses are selected.

stem: An engineer is preparing to upgrade their Cilium installation to version 1.20. According to the installation guidelines, what specific action must they take regarding the Gateway API before updating the CRDs?

options.text: Review the Gateway API v1.6.1 and TLSRoute notes in the upgrade guide.
Uninstall all existing Gateway API CRDs and reinstall them from scratch.
Switch the release channel from standard to experimental to ensure compatibility.
Verify that the TCPRoute and UDPRoute CRDs are installed to prevent data loss.

explanation: The source explicitly states that for Cilium 1.20 upgrades, one must review the Gateway API v1.6.1 and TLSRoute notes in the upgrade guide before updating Gateway API CRDs. This is part of the general advice to check the admin_upgrade for breaking changes.

optionRationale.b: The source does not recommend uninstalling and reinstalling CRDs; it advises reviewing the upgrade guide for breaking changes.
optionRationale.c: The release channel choice depends on feature needs (e.g., experimental features), not specifically on the upgrade process for version 1.20.
optionRationale.d: TCPRoute and UDPRoute are optional CRDs. Their absence disables specific features but is not a prerequisite for the upgrade process described.

stem: A cluster administrator requires the use of HTTPRoute Retry, a feature currently marked as experimental. Which release channel of the Gateway API CRDs must be installed to support this functionality?

options.text: The standard release channel, as it includes all stable features.
The experimental release channel, which includes standard features plus experimental resources.
The optional release channel, which contains only non-standard CRDs.
No specific channel is required, as HTTPRoute Retry is part of the core Gateway API.

explanation: The excerpt notes that the experimental release channel includes everything in the standard channel plus experimental resources. It specifically cites HTTPRoute Retry as an example of an experimental feature that requires installing the corresponding CRDs from this channel.

optionRationale.a: The standard channel does not include experimental features like HTTPRoute Retry.
optionRationale.c: There is no 'optional release channel' mentioned; optional CRDs are a separate set of resources (TCPRoute, UDPRoute, ListenerSet) that can be installed regardless of the channel.
optionRationale.d: HTTPRoute Retry is explicitly marked as experimental, so it is not part of the core/standard set.

citations.title: Installation
citations.quote: Note that the **experimental** release channel includes everything in the **standard** release channel plus some experimental resources and fields. If you need a feature that is currently marked as *experimental* (for example, HTTPRoute Retry in the ``HTTPRoute`` resource), you must install the corresponding CRDs.

stem: Which of the following lists contains only CRDs that are explicitly stated as required for installation from the Gateway API?

options.text: GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute, GRPCRoute, BackendTLSPolicy, ReferenceGrant, and TLSRoute.
TCPRoute, UDPRoute, ListenerSet, GatewayClass, and Gateway.
HTTPRoute, GRPCRoute, TCPRoute, UDPRoute, and ListenerSet.
Gateway, HTTPRoute, TLSRoute, TCPRoute, and UDPRoute.

explanation: The source lists GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute, GRPCRoute, BackendTLSPolicy, ReferenceGrant, and TLSRoute as the CRDs that 'must' be installed. TCPRoute, UDPRoute, and ListenerSet are listed separately as optional.

optionRationale.b: TCPRoute, UDPRoute, and ListenerSet are optional, not required.
optionRationale.c: TCPRoute, UDPRoute, and ListenerSet are optional, not required.
optionRationale.d: TCPRoute and UDPRoute are optional, not required.

stem: An engineer installs the required Gateway API CRDs but does not install the TCPRoute, UDPRoute, or ListenerSet CRDs. What is the consequence for the Cilium Gateway API controller regarding these specific features?

options.text: Cilium will disable support for these features.
Cilium will automatically install the missing CRDs upon startup.
The installation will fail because these CRDs are mandatory for the controller to start.
Cilium will use the standard release channel CRDs to emulate these features.

explanation: The source states that TCPRoute, UDPRoute, and ListenerSet CRDs are optional. If they are not installed, Cilium will disable support for these features.

optionRationale.b: The source does not state that Cilium automatically installs missing optional CRDs.
optionRationale.c: These CRDs are optional, so their absence does not cause the installation to fail.
optionRationale.d: The source does not mention emulation of features via the standard channel; it states support is disabled.

stem: An engineer runs `kubectl get gateway -A` and observes that the `PROGRAMMED` column is empty for a Gateway named `http-gateway`. The `CLASS` is `cilium` and an `ADDRESS` is present. According to the provided documentation, what is the most likely cause and the recommended action?

options.text: The Gateway API CRDs are not installed; the engineer should install the CRDs.
Gateway API is not enabled in the Cilium configuration; the engineer should ensure it is enabled.
The LoadBalancer implementation is missing; the engineer should install a LoadBalancer service.
The Gateway class is incorrect; the engineer should change the class to `envoy`.

explanation: The excerpt states: 'If the `Programmed true` indicator is missing, make sure that Gateway API is enabled in the Cilium configuration.' Since the address is present, the LoadBalancer is likely fine, and the class is correct, the missing programmed status points to the configuration setting.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states that if the resource type is not found, CRDs should be checked, but a missing 'Programmed' indicator specifically points to the Cilium configuration.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that if no IP appears (address missing), a LoadBalancer implementation might be missing. Here, an address is present.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states Cilium only programs Gateways with the class `cilium`. The class is already `cilium`, so this is not the issue.

citations.title: Checking resources
citations.quote: If the ``Programmed true`` indicator is missing, make sure that Gateway API is enabled in the Cilium configuration.

stem: A user runs `kubectl describe gateway <name>` and sees a condition with `Type: Programmed`, `Status: True`, and `Reason: Programmed`. What does this specific condition indicate about the Gateway?

options.text: The Gateway configuration was accepted by the controller.
All referenced secrets were found and have permission for use.
The Gateway configuration was programmed into Envoy.
The Gateway has been successfully scheduled.

explanation: The excerpt explicitly defines the condition types: '`Programmed`: the Gateway configuration was programmed into Envoy.'

optionRationale.a: This corresponds to the `Accepted` condition type, not `Programmed`.
optionRationale.b: This corresponds to the `ResolvedRefs` condition type, not `Programmed`.
optionRationale.d: While 'successfully scheduled' appears in the message for the `Accepted` condition in the example output, the definition of the `Programmed` condition is specifically about programming into Envoy.

citations.title: Checking resources
citations.quote: ``Programmed``: the Gateway configuration was programmed into Envoy.

stem: An engineer is troubleshooting an HTTPRoute and runs `kubectl describe httproute <name>`. They observe a condition with `Type: ResolvedRefs` and `Status: False`. According to the documentation, what does this indicate?

options.text: The HTTPRoute configuration was incorrect and rejected.
The referenced services were not found or are invalid references.
The Gateway configuration was not programmed into Envoy.
The Gateway API CRDs are missing from the cluster.

explanation: The excerpt states regarding HTTPRoute conditions: '`ResolvedRefs`: The referenced services were found and are valid references.' Therefore, if the status is false, it implies the opposite: they were not found or are invalid.

optionRationale.a: This corresponds to the `Accepted` condition type.
optionRationale.c: This corresponds to the `Programmed` condition type, which is typically associated with the Gateway resource status, though the excerpt notes similar checking methods. However, `ResolvedRefs` specifically refers to service references for the route.
optionRationale.d: This is a cluster-level issue that would likely prevent the resource from being found or described in this manner, or would be logged in the operator logs as a missing CRD error.

citations.title: Checking resources
citations.quote: ``ResolvedRefs``: The referenced services were found and are valid references.

stem: An engineer is configuring a Cilium gateway to handle traffic from a cloud load balancer that injects the client IP into the X-Forwarded-For header. By default, how does Cilium's Envoy instance determine the trusted client address for policy enforcement?

options.text: It uses the address the connection is opened from, as the default number of trusted hops is set to 0.
It uses the first value in the X-Forwarded-For list, counting from the left.
It uses the last value in the X-Forwarded-For list, counting from the right.
It ignores the X-Forwarded-For header entirely and relies solely on the TCP source IP without any header processing.

explanation: The excerpt states that by default, Cilium sets the number of trusted hops to 0, indicating that Envoy should use the address the connection is opened from, rather than a value inside the X-Forwarded-For list.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt specifies that increasing the count uses the nth value counting from the right, not the first from the left, and the default is 0 hops (connection address).
optionRationale.c: While the logic for non-zero hops counts from the right, the default is 0 hops, which means it uses the connection address, not a value from the list.
optionRationale.d: Envoy does process the header to set X-Envoy-External-Address, but for determining the trusted client address with 0 trusted hops, it uses the connection address, not ignoring the header mechanism entirely in the context of the configuration logic described.

citations.title: Source IP Visibility
citations.quote: That is, by default Cilium sets the number of trusted hops to ``0``, indicating that Envoy should use the address the connection is opened from, rather than a value inside the ``X-Forwarded-For`` list.

stem: A developer notices that their backend service is receiving the IP address of the intermediate proxy instead of the original client IP. They are using a cloud load balancer that correctly injects the client IP into the X-Forwarded-For header. Which configuration change in the values file will force Envoy to treat the traffic as coming from the client IP encoded in that header?

options.text: Set useRemoteAddress to true in the gatewayAPI section.
Set useRemoteAddress to false in the gatewayAPI or ingressController sections.
Increase the number of trusted hops to 1 in the Envoy configuration.
Remove the X-Forwarded-For header from the incoming request before it reaches Envoy.

explanation: The excerpt explicitly states that if you trust the source to inject an X-Forwarded-For header, you can force Envoy to treat the traffic as coming from the client IP encoded in the header by setting useRemoteAddress to false in gatewayAPI or ingressController sections of values files.

optionRationale.a: Setting useRemoteAddress to true would likely maintain the default behaviour of using the remote address, whereas the excerpt specifies setting it to false to use the header value.
optionRationale.c: While increasing trusted hops affects which value in the list is used, the specific mechanism described for trusting the injected header in the context of gatewayAPI/ingressController values is setting useRemoteAddress to false.
optionRationale.d: Removing the header would prevent Envoy from seeing the client IP, which is the opposite of the desired outcome.

citations.title: Source IP Visibility
citations.quote: If you trust the source of the traffic to inject an ``X-Forwarded-For`` header (such as when using a cloud load balancer), you can force Envoy to treat the traffic as coming from the client IP encoded in the ``X-Forwarded-For`` header by setting ``useRemoteAddress`` to ``false`` in ``gatewayAPI`` or ``ingressController`` sections of values files.

stem: In the context of Cilium's Envoy configuration, what is the effect of increasing the number of trusted hops from the default value?

options.text: Envoy will use the nth value from the X-Forwarded-For list, counting from the right.
Envoy will use the nth value from the X-Forwarded-For list, counting from the left.
Envoy will ignore the X-Forwarded-For header and always use the TCP source address.
Envoy will append the new hop count to the X-Forwarded-For header before forwarding the request.

explanation: The excerpt states that increasing the count will have Envoy use the nth value from the list, counting from the right.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly states the counting is from the right, not the left.
optionRationale.c: Increasing the count specifically directs Envoy to look at the list, rather than ignoring it.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes how the trusted address is determined, not how the header is modified for forwarding (though appending is mentioned as a general action, the specific effect of the hop count is on selection).

citations.title: Source IP Visibility
citations.quote: Increasing this count will have Envoy use the ``n`` th value from the list, counting from the right.

stem: Which header does Envoy set to the trusted client address, based on the X-Forwarded-For header, regardless of what that address turns out to be?

options.text: X-Forwarded-For
X-Envoy-External-Address
X-Real-IP
X-Client-IP

explanation: The excerpt states that Envoy will also set the X-Envoy-External-Address header to the trusted client address, whatever that turns out to be, based on X-Forwarded-For.

optionRationale.a: X-Forwarded-For is the header that is appended to or read from, not the one set to the trusted client address by Envoy in this specific context.
optionRationale.c: X-Real-IP is not mentioned in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: X-Client-IP is not mentioned in the excerpt.

citations.title: Source IP Visibility
citations.quote: Envoy will also set the ``X-Envoy-External-Address`` header to the trusted client address, whatever that turns out to be, based on ``X-Forwarded-For``.
